full_text_en:
Fenghai Company v. Hainan PICC

Dispute over Marine Cargo Insurance Contract

[Ruling Summary]

An insurance policy is a typical standard-form contract. The insurer, as the party providing the standard-form contract, shall determine the rights and obligations of the parties in accordance with the principle of fairness and shall adopt reasonable means to draw the attention of the other party to the clauses that exclude the insurer's liability; otherwise, such exclusion clauses shall be invalid.

Under a marine cargo insurance contract, the "all risks" coverage stipulated in the "Ocean Marine Cargo Insurance Clauses" includes, in addition to the liabilities under Free from Particular Average (FPA) and With Average (WA), all loss of or damage to the insured cargo caused by external causes during the course of transit. In the absence of intentional misconduct or negligence on the part of the insured, unless the loss of the insured cargo falls within the exclusions stipulated in the insurance contract, the insurer shall be liable for all losses caused by external causes during the course of transit.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2003) Min Si Ti Zi No. 5

Re-applicant (Original Defendant at First Instance): Hainan Fenghai Grain and Oil Industry Co., Ltd. Address: Room 306, Fenghuang Building, Yilong Road, Haikou City, Hainan Province.

Legal Representative: Zhang Jinrong, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Li Lei, Attorney at Beijing Kangda Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Weng Jusong, Attorney at Beijing Kangda Law Firm, Hainan Branch.

Original Appellant at First Instance: Property and Casualty Company Limited, Hainan Province Branch (formerly: Zhongbao Property Insurance Company Limited, Hainan Province Branch). Address: No. 22, Binhai Avenue, Haikou City, Hainan Province.

Litigation Representative: Li Jianhua, Deputy General Manager of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Zhong Cheng, Attorney at Guangdong Jinghai Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Xu Jianfeng, Attorney at Guangdong Jinghai Law Firm.

In the case of Hainan Fenghai Grain and Oil Industry Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Fenghai Company) v. Zhongbao Property Insurance Company Limited, Hainan Province Branch (hereinafter referred to as Hainan PICC) concerning a dispute over a marine cargo insurance contract, the Hainan High People's Court rendered the Civil Judgment (1997) Qiong Jing Zhong Zi No. 44 on October 27, 1997, which has become legally effective. Dissatisfied with the above judgment, Fenghai Company filed a petition for retrial with this Court. This Court referred the case to the Hainan High People's Court for review. After review, that court rendered a decision on December 3, 2001, rejecting Fenghai Company's petition for retrial. Fenghai Company, on the ground that the final judgment of the original trial erroneously applied insurance law, leading to an erroneous judgment, again filed a petition for retrial with this Court. By Civil Ruling (2003) Min Si Jian Zi No. 35 dated August 11, 2003, this Court decided to conduct a retrial of this case. This Court lawfully formed a collegial panel and held a public hearing in this case. The agents ad litem of the re-applicant Fenghai Company, Li Lei and Weng Jusong, and the agents ad litem of the original appellant Hainan PICC, Zhong Cheng and Xu Jianfeng, appeared before the court to participate in the proceedings. This case is now concluded.

The original trial found: On November 28, 1995, Fenghai Company insured with Hainan PICC 4,999.85 tons of palm oil in drums shipped by the Indonesian vessel "HAGAAG" from Dumai Port, Indonesia to Yangpu Port, China. The insurance coverage was All Risks, the cargo value was USD 3,574,892.75, the insured amount was USD 3,951,258, and the premium was USD 18,966. After insuring, Fenghai Company paid the insurance premium to Hainan PICC as agreed. Hainan PICC issued a dispatch notice to Fenghai Company and signed and issued a marine cargo insurance policy, attaching the Ocean Marine Cargo Insurance Clauses to the policy. According to the insurance clauses, the coverage scope of All Risks includes, in addition to the liabilities under FPA and WA, that Hainan PICC is also "liable for all loss of or damage to the insured cargo caused by external causes during the course of transit." The clauses also stipulate five items of exclusions. The above insured cargo was purchased by Fenghai Company from Singapore Wilmar Private Limited (hereinafter referred to as Wilmar) on CNF terms. Under the sales contract, the shipper Wilmar entered into a charter party with the shipowner's agent Liang International Agency Limited (hereinafter referred to as Liang International). The charter party stipulated that the vessel "HAGAAG" would carry the 5,000 tons of palm oil insured by Fenghai Company to Yangpu Port, China, and another 1,000 tons of palm oil to Hong Kong. On November 29, 1995, the time charterer of the "HAGAAG" and the actual carrier of the cargo, PT SAMUDERA INDRA Company of Indonesia (hereinafter referred to as PSI Company), issued a shipped bill of lading numbered DM/YPU/1490/95, which indicated the vessel as "HAGAAG", the port of loading as Dumai Port, Indonesia, the port of discharge as Yangpu Port, China, the cargo mark as BATCH NO. 80211/95, the quantity loaded as 4,999.85 tons, clean on board, freight prepaid. It was found that the shipper Wilmar paid the freight to Liang International, and Liang International had paid the freight to PSI Company. On December 14, 1995, Fenghai Company paid the issuing bank and took delivery of the documents, obtaining the full set (3 originals) of the bills of lading for the above insured cargo.

From November 23 to 29, 1995, after the "HAGAAG" loaded 31,623 drums, net weight 5,999.82 tons, of Four Seas brand palm oil at Dumai Port and set sail, due to a dispute over the hire of the vessel between the owner of the "HAGAAG", PT. PERUSAHAAN PELAYARAN BAHTERA BINTANG SELATAN Company of Indonesia (hereinafter referred to as BBS Company), and the time charterer PSI Company, the "HAGAAG" interrupted the voyage stipulated in the bill of lading and blocked the disclosure of the vessel's whereabouts. To avoid loss of the insured cargo, the shipper Wilmar, Fenghai Company, and Hainan PICC sent representatives multiple times to participate in negotiations between the owner of the "HAGAAG" and the time charterer. However, the shipowner refused to disclose the whereabouts of the "HAGAAG" on the grounds of not having received the hire, and the multi-party talks were fruitless. Thereafter, Wilmar and Fenghai Company communicated through various channels and searched for the whereabouts of the "HAGAAG", and Hainan PICC also assisted in the search through its overseas offices. It was not until April 1996 that the truth was revealed when the "HAGAAG" smuggled into Shanwei, China, and was seized by the Chinese Coast Guard. According to the determination in the "Decision on Exemption from Prosecution" (Sui Jian Xing Mian Zi [1996] No. 64) issued by the Guangzhou People's Procuratorate, from January to March 1996, Captain Ellis Lumbakang of the "HAGAAG", acting on instructions from BBS Company, directed the crew to transship 11,325 drums, over 2,100 tons, of palm oil onto "Iwana" and "Salaha" cargo vessels belonging to the same shipping company for removal and sale, and also had the crew paint over the name "HAGAAG" and rename the vessel "ELIZA II". In April 1996, the renamed "ELIZA II" carried the remaining 20,298 drums of palm oil smuggled into Shanwei, China, and was seized by the Chinese Coast Guard on April 16. The above 20,298 drums of palm oil were confiscated and turned over to the state treasury by the Guangdong Provincial Procuratorial Authority as smuggled goods. On June 6, 1996, Fenghai Company submitted a claim report to Hainan PICC. On August 20, 1996, Fenghai Company again submitted a written claim application to Hainan PICC. Hainan PICC explicitly refused to pay the claim. Fenghai Company then filed a lawsuit with the Haikou Maritime Court.

The original trial further found: Fenghai Company was a Sino-foreign equity joint venture established on August 14, 1995, by Hainan Fengyuan Trade Development Co., Ltd. and Singapore Haiyuan International Co., Ltd. After its establishment, it established a business relationship with Hainan PICC. From October 1, 1995, to November 28, 1995 (before the issuance of the insurance policy in this case), there were four insurance transactions for imported palm oil, of which three were insured under All Risks, and one was "All Risks with War Risks attached." Claims were made for all four insurance transactions, including payments for shortages and leakage of cargo within the scope of All Risks.

The original trial also found: In accordance with the spirit of the People's Bank of China Document Yin Fu (1996) No. 248, the People's Insurance Company of China, Hainan Province Branch was dissolved on August 16, 1996, and Zhongbao Property Insurance Company Limited, Hainan Province Branch and Zhongbao Life Insurance Company Limited, Hainan Province Branch were established separately. Zhongbao Property Insurance Company Limited, Hainan Province Branch obtained its business license from the Hainan Provincial Administration for Industry and Commerce on September 23, 1996. According to the relevant provisions of Yin Fu (1996) No. 248 and the "Articles of Association of Zhongbao Property Insurance Company Limited", the property insurance business of Hainan PICC was assumed by Hainan Caibao.

The above facts are confirmed by the insurance policy, dispatch notice, Ocean Marine Cargo Insurance Clauses, sales contract, cargo transportation contract, original bill of lading, freight payment vouchers, acceptance drafts, communications via fax between the parties, relevant letters, claim application, payment vouchers, decision on exemption from prosecution, notice of rejection of petition, documents from the People's Bank of China, business license, articles of association, and other evidence, which were admitted and verified through cross-examination during the first instance trial by the Haikou Maritime Court and the second instance trial by the Hainan High People's Court.

The Haikou Maritime Court held that: The insurance contract concluded between Fenghai Company and Hainan PICC is valid, and the rights and obligations of the parties shall be governed and adjusted by the insurance policy and the attached insurance clauses. Regarding the insured cargo involved in this case, 3,848.07 tons were treated as smuggled goods by the Chinese border defense authorities due to the smuggling activities of the shipowner BBS Company, and the remaining cargo was illegally sold by the shipowner; neither can be recovered by Fenghai Company. In accordance with Article 245 of the Maritime Code of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Maritime Code), the insured subject matter in this case has incurred a total loss; The shipper Wilmar's act of entering into a voyage charter party with Liang International was in compliance with legal provisions and customary practices of international trade transportation, and the freight payment vouchers presented by Wilmar in court and the notation "freight prepaid" on the bill of lading issued by the actual carrier PSI Company both prove that the shipper had fulfilled its obligation to pay the freight for the voyage; therefore, the shipper is not liable for the loss of the insured subject matter in this case; In this case, Fenghai Company, when the carrying vessel "HAGAAG" did not arrive at the agreed port of discharge within a reasonable time, notified Hainan PICC in writing and took necessary and reasonable measures, actively acting to prevent or mitigate the loss of the insured subject matter; therefore, Fenghai Company is not negligent or at fault for the loss of the insured subject matter. The loss of the insured subject matter in this case was caused by the theft, sale, and smuggling activities of the shipowner BBS Company of the "HAGAAG". According to the insurance clauses attached to the policy involved in this case, this falls under "external causes" that Fenghai Company could not predict or control, meeting the coverage conditions of the All Risks insurance purchased by Fenghai Company. Hainan PICC's argument that the loss of the insured subject matter in this case was based on commercial and social risk, and that if Fenghai Company wished to obtain insurance coverage, it should have purchased a specially agreed risk type, such as "Failure to Deliver Risk", is not supported because such risk is not listed in the exclusions of the insurance clauses and was not clearly stated when concluding the insurance contract, violating Article 16 of the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Insurance Law), which states "When concluding an insurance contract, the insurer shall explain the contents of the insurance contract to the applicant" and Article 17, which states "If the insurance contract contains clauses regarding the insurer's exemption from liability, the insurer shall clearly explain them to the applicant at the time of concluding the contract; if such explanation is not clearly given, the clauses shall have no effect." Therefore, its above argument is not supported.

The Haikou Maritime Court held that: Hainan PICC's argument that the insured subject matter had not yet incurred an actual total loss, that the loss claimed by Fenghai Company fell within the exclusions and was not within the scope of coverage, and that it should therefore be exempted from compensation liability, lacks factual and legal basis and is not supported. Fenghai Company has fulfilled its legal and contractual obligations as the insured. When its insured cargo suffers losses within the scope of coverage stipulated in the insurance contract, it is entitled to obtain insurance compensation in accordance with the contract. Therefore, Fenghai Company's claim that Hainan PICC should compensate for the loss of the insured subject matter in accordance with the contract is supported. Since Fenghai Company and Hainan PICC did not agree on the insured value when concluding the insurance contract, in accordance with Article 219, Paragraph 2, Item 3 of the Maritime Code, the calculation should be based on the cargo value (including freight) plus insurance premium for the insured cargo in this case, i.e., the insured value of the insured subject matter in this case is USD 3,593,858.75. Fenghai Company's claim for compensation for expenses incurred to prevent and mitigate the loss of the insured subject matter lacks sufficient evidence and is not supported. After deliberation by the judicial committee of the Haikou Maritime Court, and in accordance with Article 106 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 237 of the Maritime Code, and Article 23 of the Insurance Law, it is adjudged that: Hainan PICC shall compensate Fenghai Company USD 3,593,858.75 for the loss of the insured value; all other claims of Fenghai Company are dismissed.

The Hainan High People's Court held that: The insurance contract concluded between Hainan PICC and Fenghai Company is legally valid, and the rights and obligations of the parties shall be governed by the insurance policy and the attached insurance clauses. Since Hainan PICC was dissolved during the litigation, and its property insurance business has been assumed by Hainan Caibao, the appellant in this case should be changed to Hainan Caibao. The insured subject matter in this case has incurred an actual total loss, and the shipper Wilmar is not at fault or liable for the loss of the insured subject matter. The loss of the insured subject matter in this case was caused by the shipowner BBS Company's removal and sale of the cargo carried by the "HAGAAG" and its smuggling activities. According to the insurance clauses attached to the insurance policy and the customs of the insurance industry, the scope of liability for All Risks includes FPA, WA, and general additional risks (i.e., Theft, Pilferage, and Non-Delivery (TPND); Fresh Water and/or Rain Damage; Shortage; Contamination; Leakage; Clashing and Breakage; Taint of Odor; Sweating and Heating; Hook Damage; Breakage of Packing; and Rusting). The People's Bank of China's "Reply to the Request for Interpretation of the Ocean Marine Cargo 'All Risks' Clause" also makes the same explicit provision. It can be seen that the loss of the cargo insured by Fenghai Company does not fall within the scope of liability for All Risks. Furthermore, given the long-term insurance business relationship between Hainan PICC and Fenghai Company, and that before the occurrence of the dispute in this case, the parties had concluded multiple insurance contracts, and Hainan PICC had even made compensation within the scope of All Risks, Fenghai Company should have been clear about the main contents of the insurance contract in this case, the exemption clauses, and the scope of liability for All Risks. Therefore, the first instance judgment's decision to hold Hainan PICC liable for compensation on the grounds that the loss of the insured subject matter fell within the scope of liability for All Risks and that Hainan PICC had failed to fulfill its obligation of explanation is improper. The first instance judgment was unclear in its finding of fact regarding the occurrence of an actual total loss of the insured subject matter and erroneous in its application of law, and should be corrected. The grounds of appeal raised by Hainan PICC are valid and should be supported. However, Hainan PICC failed to fully fulfill its burden of proof during the first instance, causing unnecessary litigation, and shall bear the litigation costs for the second instance. After deliberation and decision by the judicial committee of the Hainan High People's Court, it is adjudged to set aside the first instance judgment and dismiss all claims of Fenghai Company.

The grounds for Fenghai Company's petition for retrial are: The final judgment of the original trial was indeed erroneous in its application of China's insurance law, and thereby clearly violated legal provisions in its determination of the insurer's exemption clauses. Specifically: The determination that the insured cargo did not fall within the scope of liability for All Risks clearly exceeded the explicit agreement on "exclusions" in the "Ocean Marine Cargo Insurance Clauses" involved in this case. The "Ocean Marine Cargo Insurance Clauses" did not explicitly agree in writing that the scope of liability for All Risks includes FPA, WA, and general additional risks; The insurer and its insurance business representatives never explained the scope of All Risks to Fenghai Company, let alone explained the scope of liability for "Non-Delivery Risk". When Fenghai Company insured 4,999.85 tons of palm oil under All Risks and Hainan PICC issued the dispatch notice and insurance policy, the insurer and its insurance business representatives never explained to the applicant that "external causes" did not include the shipowner directing the captain and crew to arbitrarily sell the cargo carried by the vessel during the voyage, nor did they explain that it did not include the Chinese Coast Guard detaining and confiscating the cargo carried by the vessel; The five items of insurer exemption explicitly stipulated in the insurance clauses by the applicant and the insurer do not include the insured subject matter being sold by the captain and crew or being confiscated by the Chinese Border Control Armed Police in this case; The final judgment's arbitrary expansion of the loss of the subject matter in this case to the scope of the insurer's exemption not only clearly violates the insurance clauses but also clearly violates the relevant provisions of China's insurance law. According to the Insurance Law, clauses that are not clearly explained at the time of concluding the insurance contract shall have no effect. Where there is a dispute between the insurer and the applicant, insured, or beneficiary regarding the terms of the insurance contract, the people's court or arbitration institution shall make an interpretation favorable to the insured and beneficiary. The final judgment's reliance on the People's Bank of China's reply as the basis for its decision is improper; Hainan PICC had never compensated or refused to compensate Fenghai Company for a loss of the type of insured subject matter in this case. The fact that Hainan PICC had previously compensated Fenghai Company for WA coverage does not mean that Hainan PICC had clearly informed Fenghai Company at the time of concluding the insurance contract in this case that the situation in this case fell within the exemption scope. The final judgment should have found an actual total loss of the insured subject matter in this case. Fenghai Company requests this Court to conduct a retrial.

Hainan PICC responded in its defense: 1. The scope of retrial review should be limited to whether the final judgment of the original trial was erroneous in its application of law; 2. The final judgment of the original trial was not erroneous in its application of law; this case should be governed by the Maritime Code and the 1995 Insurance Law; 3. The final judgment's determination that the loss of the insured subject matter did not fall within the insurance coverage scope has sufficient legal basis: The Ocean Marine Cargo Insurance Clauses involved in this case were formulated and promulgated by a competent state administrative authority and have the nature of administrative regulations. The Ocean Marine Cargo All Risks clause is a specified risk clause, not an open-ended clause covering everything except "exclusions". Its scope of insurance liability refers only to FPA, WA, plus 11 additional risks, i.e., the "external causes" in All Risks refer only to the external causes listed in the 11 additional risks; 4. The cause of the loss of the insured subject matter in this case was the shipowner's misappropriation and government confiscation, not any natural calamity or accident. The loss of the insured subject matter in this case does not fall within the scope of liability for All Risks; 5. This case does not involve the issue of exclusions. Since the loss does not fall within the scope of liability of the statutory insurance clauses, the principle of adverse interpretation under Article 30 of the Insurance Law is not applicable to this case. Hainan PICC did not violate any legal obligations imposed on the insurer. It requests that Fenghai Company's petition for retrial be dismissed and the final judgment of the original trial be upheld.

During the retrial before this Court, neither party submitted new evidence material, nor raised any objection to the facts found in the original trial, which are hereby affirmed by this Court.

It was further found that: The People's Bank of China's "Reply to the Request for Interpretation of the Ocean Marine Cargo 'All Risks' Clause" was provided by Hainan PICC to the court during the second instance; In accordance with the spirit of the Reply Bao Jian Fu [2003] No. 117 of the China Insurance Regulatory Commission, Zhongbao Property Insurance Company Limited, Hainan Province Branch changed its name to Property and Casualty Company Limited, Hainan Province Branch on August 12, 2003.

This Court holds that: This case is a dispute over an international marine cargo insurance contract. The insured, the port of destination of the insured cargo, etc., are all within the territory of the People's Republic of China. The original trial correctly applied the law of the People's Republic of China as the governing law for resolving this dispute, and neither party objects to this.

The insurance contract concluded between Fenghai Company and Hainan PICC was lawful and valid, and the rights and obligations of both parties shall be governed by the insurance policy and the attached insurance clauses. The subject matter insured under this case had already suffered actual total loss. In this regard, the shipper Fengyi Company was not at fault, nor was there any evidence showing that the insured Fenghai Company acted intentionally or negligently. The loss of the subject matter insured was caused by the freight dispute between Bareboat Company (BBS), the owner of the vessel "Haka," and the time charterer, who subsequently removed, sold, and smuggled the cargo on board. The focus of the dispute in this case lies in how to understand the scope of coverage of "all risks" under the insurance clauses involved.

According to the provisions of the "Ocean Marine Cargo Insurance Clauses" under this case, all risks "include, in addition to the liabilities covered under Free from Particular Average (FPA) and With Average (WA) insurance, all loss of or damage to the insured goods caused by external causes during the course of transit." The insurance clauses also list five exclusion clauses applicable to the insurer, namely: (1) Loss caused by the intentional act or negligence of the insured; (2) Loss caused by the liability of the shipper; (3) Loss caused by defective quality or shortage in quantity of the insured goods existing prior to the attachment of insurance liability; (4) Loss caused by natural wear and tear, inherent defect, nature of the insured goods, market decline, or delay in transit; (5) The scope of coverage and exclusions as stipulated in the Company's Ocean Marine Cargo War Risks Clauses and Cargo Strike Clauses. From the provisions of the insurance clauses in this case, except for the five exclusion clauses mentioned above, the insurer shall bear liability for losses under FPA and WA, as well as losses caused by various external causes during the course of transit of the insured goods.

What constitutes an "external cause" during transit pertains to the interpretation of the insurance clauses. An insurance contract, being a type of standard form contract, requires the party providing the standard terms to define the rights and obligations between the parties in accordance with the principle of fairness, draw the other party's attention in a reasonable manner to clauses that exempt or limit its liability, and, upon the other party's request, explain such clauses. The exclusion clauses in the insurance clauses of this case do not include loss of the subject matter insured caused by the carrier's illegal act of stealing and selling the entire cargo or smuggling. Hainan PICC also could not prove that, at the time of concluding the insurance contract, it had explained to Fenghai Company that losses caused by the carrier's illegal act of stealing and selling the entire cargo or smuggling were not within the scope of insurance coverage. Therefore, Hainan PICC shall bear the liability for compensation in accordance with the contract. The court of first instance found that, given the long-term insurance business relationship between Hainan PICC and Fenghai Company, and that before the dispute in this case arose, the parties had entered into multiple insurance contracts and Hainan PICC had even made payments under the all risks coverage, Fenghai Company was deemed to be clear about the main contents, exclusion clauses, and scope of all risks coverage of the insurance contract in this case. Based on this, Hainan PICC could be exempted from compensation liability for this case. This finding lacks factual and legal basis and shall be corrected.

Hainan PICC provided to the court of first instance a reply letter from the People's Bank of China to the People's Insurance Company of China (Group), interpreting the "all risks" clause, to prove that the incident in this case was not within the scope of insurance coverage. This Court is of the opinion that, according to the provisions of the Insurance Law of China, the insurer shall explain the contents of the insurance contract clauses to the applicant at the time of concluding the insurance contract. The People's Bank of China, as the competent authority of the insurance industry at the time, issued an interpretation of the insurance contract clauses after the occurrence of the insured incident in this case, which should not apply to this case. Furthermore, from the reply letter of the People's Bank of China, it cannot be concluded that the incident in this case does not fall within the scope of all risks coverage.

In summary, this Court finds that the loss of the subject matter insured in this case does not fall under the exclusion clauses stipulated in the insurance clauses. It was caused by external factors beyond the control of the consignee, the insured Fenghai Company. Therefore, the insured incident in this case shall be deemed to be within the scope of all risks coverage. The court of first instance erroneously found that the loss of the goods insured by Fenghai Company was not within the scope of all risks coverage, and this shall be corrected. The grounds for retrial application of Fenghai Company are well-founded and shall be supported. Pursuant to Article 184, paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, this Court hereby renders the following judgment:

1. The civil judgment (1997) Qiong Jing Zhong Zi No. 44 of the Hainan High People's Court is set aside;

2. The civil judgment (1996) Hai Shang Chu Zi No. 096 of the Haikou Maritime Court is affirmed.

Court acceptance fees for first and second instance, each in the amount of RMB 184,674, shall be borne by the Hainan Branch of the People's Property Insurance Company of China Limited.

This judgment is final.

Presiding Judge: Wang Shumei

Judge: Liu Shoujie

Acting Judge: Hu Fang

July 13, 2004

Clerk: Fu Xiaoqiang (acting)
